newsitem.title: THAILAND: Ruby trade flourishes in former Khmer Rouge area.
newsitem.headline: Ruby trade flourishes in former Khmer Rouge area.

text.p: Former Khmer Rouge guerrillas, who defected to the Cambodian government last year, are still making millions of dollars selling rubies to Thai dealers, gem industry sources said on Monday.

There were at least 29 ruby mining companies in the area around the former Khmer Rouge stronghold of Pailin in western Cambodia, said a manager of a Thai ruby firm based in neighbouring eastern Thai Chantaburi province.
"Each company has to pay 220,000 baht ($8,800) per month to the dissident faction," the manager, who declined to be identified, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

The main beneficiary of the ruby trade was still the former Khmer Rouge commander of the Pailin area, Ei Chien, whose faction broke away from the hardline Maoist Khmer Rouge core group led by supremo Pol Pot last August.
Ei Chien defected to the government side with Ieng Sary, who was foreign minister in the Khmer Rouge during its 1975-1979 rule of terror.
More than a million Cambodians died of starvation, torture, disease or overwork during the rebels' campaign of radical agrarian reform.
Thai businessmen continued to deal and pay Ei Chien directly for gems although Cambodian government troops were stationed in Pailin, the manager added.
The number of ruby mines was expected to increase with reports of Singapore and Hong Kong businessmen joining the trade, he said.

"We have learned that the businessmen from Singapore and Hong Kong have bought many plots of land in Pailin and they are poised to come into the ruby mining business but we don't have much detail," he said.
There were more than 120 active ruby miners around Pailin before the United Nations banned ruby and logging exports from then-Khmer Rouge controlled areas in January 1993.
Until then, the Chamber of Commerce in Chantaburi, which borders Pailin, estimated the Khmer Rouge were posting gains of at least $40 million a month from ruby and log sales to Thai businessmen.
Dissident Khmer Rouge sources said that they had benefited from their defection to the Cambodian government, but declined to comment on the ruby business.
"Our living conditions have improved a lot after we merged our troops with the government's," a former Khmer Rouge officer in Pailin said by telephone.
Despite the merger, the dissident faction was in full control of Pailin's administration and had also benefited from cheaper food, he added.

"We used to rely on all the consumer products from Thailand," he said. "But now we have switched to buy cheaper foods including rice, fish and vagetables from inside Cambodia and contraband from Phnom Penh."
